title: Body Size, Radiation Dose and Exposure Index in Conventional Radiography: A Multicentre Prospective Study
content: Background/Objectives: The exposure index (EI) reflects detector exposure rather than patient dose, but its behaviour with increasing patient size remains incompletely characterised across radiographic examinations. We evaluated continuous associations of body mass index (BMI) and regional body thickness with dose–area product (DAP), entrance surface dose (ESD), and EI, and tested whether associations differed by examination and institution. Methods: This prospective multicentre observational study included 572 exposures from 331 adults undergoing nine projections at three institutions. Generalised estimating equations with a Gamma distribution and log link accounted for repeated exposures and adjusted for examination, institution, log mAs, kVp, source-to-skin distance, age, and sex. Results: Each 1 kg/m² increase in BMI was associated with a 5.30% lower EI (95% CI, 4.53–6.08%; p < 0.001) and a 1.15% higher DAP (95% CI, 0.29–2.01%; p = 0.008), but not with ESD. Each 1 cm increase in regional thickness was associated with a 4.26% lower EI (95% CI, 3.27–5.24%; p < 0.001) and a 0.19% higher ESD (95% CI, 0.02–0.35%; p = 0.026), but not with DAP. ESD and EI associations varied by examination (interaction p < 0.001), and institutional differences persisted after adjustment. Conclusions: Body-size associations were outcome-specific and examination-specific. The strong inverse EI associations, despite modest adjusted patient-dose associations, show that EI should not be used as a surrogate for patient dose. Optimisation should use examination- and system-specific EI interpretation alongside body size, technical factors, and patient-dose indicators.
